name: OpenAPI Search
license: MIT (MCP server); the directory repository has no license file
summary: A small, open directory of OpenAPI descriptions for popular APIs, with an MCP server that turns any of them, or any spec URL, into a short plain-language summary an AI model can read before writing calls.
intro: OpenAPI Search is a one-person open-source project by Jan Wilmake. Its core is a hand-curated `providers.json` that maps about 66 short ids, such as `stripe`, `github`, `supabase` or `hackernews`, to the URL of each API’s OpenAPI file, and `https://openapisearch.com/redirect/<id>` sends you to that file. The site also serves the list as Markdown and `llms.txt`, so a model can read the whole directory in one request.

The useful part for agents is the companion MCP server, a Cloudflare Worker reachable at `https://openapi-mcp.openapisearch.com/mcp`. It has two tools. `getApiOverview` takes a directory id or a raw spec URL, fetches the JSON or YAML (converting old Swagger 2.0 files through swagger.io’s converter), and returns a plain-language list of the endpoints. `getApiOperation` then returns the detail for one operation by id or route. The same summaries are served over plain HTTP at oapis.org, so the model reads a short summary instead of the full spec.

It is a side project rather than a product: there is no account, pricing or service-level promise, the directory covers dozens of APIs rather than thousands, and its own README says the author chose to focus on the quality of a few great specs over quantity.
strengths: Free and open: the MCP server is MIT-licensed and runs as a single Cloudflare Worker you can deploy yourself
Works with any OpenAPI or Swagger URL, not only the curated ids
Small context cost: a model gets a summary and then one operation at a time instead of the whole spec
limits: A small, hand-maintained list of about 66 APIs, and the directory repository has no license file
Run by one person with no stated uptime or support; the summaries depend on oapis.org and swagger.io’s public converter
It only describes APIs: it does no authentication or calls, so the agent still needs keys and an HTTP tool to act

story: Jan Wilmake started the directory in January 2025 because, in their words, OpenAPI descriptions “are effectively closed if there isn’t an accessible way to find and use them”: commercial marketplaces such as RapidAPI dominated search results, and the best open directory, APIs.guru, listed only a fraction of public APIs. The goal was a registry easy for agents to navigate rather than a docs site.

In March 2025 Wilmake picked the project back up and relaunched it with a narrower aim, quality over quantity, and paired it with an MCP server so Claude and Cursor could use it. They posted it to Hacker News on 22 March 2025 as “Make APIs accessible for AI codegen”, warning readers to expect bugs. Later updates added an `llms.txt` file and a skills endpoint (January 2026) and a handful of fixes.

choices.choice: Summaries in simple language instead of raw specs
choices.why: Large OpenAPI files overflow a model’s context, so the MCP server first identifies the API, then returns an overview, then the details of only the endpoints the model needs.

choices.choice: Quality of a few specs over quantity
choices.why: Wilmake’s March 2025 changelog notes that people want to see their own APIs and aren’t interested in 99% of the others, so the project curates a short list instead of crawling for thousands.
The README lists custom, non-standard logic as a non-goal: improvements should be a layer on top of plain OpenAPI files.
